thread.title: Facebook: We're Going to Push Zuckerberg, Says New York City Comptroller

author: Barron's
title: Facebook: We're Going to Push Zuckerberg, Says New York City Comptroller
text:
Scott Stringer , New York City's comptroller, was on CNBC's "Squawk Alley" to explain why he's called for changes to Facebook 's ( FB ) board of directors.
Stringer oversees New York City's pension fund , and has close to $1 billion of Facebook stock in that fund.
"We are the fourth-largest pension fund in America," Stringer pointed out. "Part of our role is to think about how our investments are making companies stronger by asking questions that need to be asked both on this show and around the world."
Stringer said he thinks Facebook should add three independent directors , specifically ones who would have some expertise, he said, in topics of data usage and ethics.
"Data is being used without people's permission, and that's going to affect the brand," said Stringer, "and that's a brand I've invested close to $1 billion of people's money in underlying their pensions."
"They're in uncharted waters," he added, referring tof Facebook. "They have not comported themselves in a way that makes people feel good about their personal data."
Calling it a "wake-up call," Stringer said the controversy over misuse of Facebook user data by Cambridge Analytica posed "revenue risks, brand risk, and risk to our democracy."
Stringer told the show's hosts that "Congress has to ask tough questions" of Facebook management.
Stringer presented himself as part of the community of pension-fund managers who are concerned around the world. "When you start looking at what's happening throughout the world, everyone who is a fiduciary to a pension fund has an absolute right to ask questions of the board," he said.
"We are not trying to harm Facebook, we are trying to make it a stronger company," Stringer said. "We have an obligation to step up and act as a fiduciary.
"We're long-term investors in Facebook, and we're long-term investors in thousands of companies. When we see something coming, we try to go to the board to get answers for our firefighters and our teachers."
Asked by the hosts what he thinks CEO Mark Zuckerberg should do, Stringer offered, "I think, own up to some of the challenges this company is facing, as it relates to data and transferring that data to the analyst companies.
"And step up and tell the story, and explain the problems. Do not go silent, do not think this is going to go away.
"We're going to push Mr. Zuckerberg to continue to think about the company in the long term."
The drumbeat for a more active board extends beyond Wall Street. Jeremy Ring , a former Yahoo! sales executive and Florida state senator, says the Cambridge Analytica fiasco signals a point "where the board has to sit down and have a serious discussion with Zuckerberg."
Facebook's travails have prompted pointed comments from Apple ( AAPL ) CEO Tim Cook , who took it to task for its handling of consumer data, and threats of regulation in the U.S. and abroad. In a recent interview with Vox, Zuckerberg dismissed Cook's critique as "extremely glib" and "not at all aligned with the truth."
"I think it's important that we don't get all Stockholm syndrome and let the companies that work hard to charge you more convince you that they actually care about you," Zuckerberg said. "Because that sounds ridiculous to me."
Facebook shares today are down $4.60, or almost 3%, at $155.19.
